senses: Of clothing, appearance, etc., cheap and gaudy; showy.
Of a character, behavior, or situation, etc., unseemly, base, mean-spirited, shameful.
ety: Shortened from tawdry lace; originally a corruption and rebracketing of Saint Audrey lace (from Old English Æðelþrȳð). The lace necklaces sold to pilgrims to Saint Audrey fell out of fashion in the 17th century, and so tawdry was reinterpreted as meaning “cheap” or “vulgar”.
examples: This wasn't really a room for me; the green curtains before the windows were rather tawdry, and there was anything but an abundance of nails on the walls for hanging one's wardrobe.
It was all cheap and incredibly tawdry, from the festoons of paper roses on the walls to the flash of paste jewels in make-believe crowns.
The woman's passion by his side seemed suddenly tawdry and unreal, the seeking of her lips for his something horrible.

senses: One to whom an offer is made.
ety: From offer + -ee.
examples: A unilateral contract consists of a promise on the part of the offeror and performance of the requisite terms by the offeree.

senses: A soft, moist mass, usually wrapped in cloth and warmed, that is applied topically to a sore, aching or lesioned part of the body to soothe it.
A porous solid filled with solvent, used to remove stains from porous stone such as marble or granite.
ety: From Middle English pultes, from Latin pultes, plural of puls. The phonological development from Middle English is regular; compare poultry.
examples: The poultice relaxeth the pores.
Sties in the eye are irritating and disfiguring. Foment with warm water; at night apply a bread-and-milk poultice.

senses: A college course designed to give a student supervised practical knowledge of a subject previously studied theoretically.
A science exam in which students are questioned about specimens or other objects placed in front of them.
ety: Borrowed from German Praktikum, a coinage from the neuter of Late Latin practicus (“practical”), from Ancient Greek πρακτικός (praktikós, “of or pertaining to action, concerned with action or business, active, practical”), from πράσσω (prássō, “to do”).
examples: Eromin has provided clinical practicum placements for students seeking advanced degrees in social service professions.

senses: An eight-line poem whose rhyme scheme is ABaAabAB and whose lines are in iambic tetrameter.
ety: Borrowed from French triolet.
examples: The triolet, like the sestina and several other forms of French-derived poetry, is a form of rhyming poetry that has lines that repeat.

senses: Directly opposing.
ety: 1802, probably shortened from diametrical (1550s).
examples: In some religions, good and evil are considered diametric opposites.

senses: A ravine or valley in Latin America.
ety: Borrowed from Spanish quebrada.
examples: Later, friends told me of the dangers of absorbing fright illness and mal aire from the quebrada, especially from eggs and other curing paraphernalia discarded there.

senses: Tasty, nice, fun, great.
Good in a generic sense, worthy, functional.
ety: From Afrikaans lekker, from Dutch lekker.
examples: There were 2 000 rounds of ammo to fire between us four loadies. We sat there for hours and took our potshots. It was kiff; the R5 was a lekker thing.
The other men ask why he's crying, when he's got such a lekker car. The guy shakes his head and says, "I just saw my wife, and she was driving a skateboard."

senses: Wearing jackboots.
Authoritarian or oppressive, especially in a cruel or violent manner.
ety: From jackboot + -ed.
examples: In the departure zone he rasped at Lufthansa officials in what seemed very theatrical German. So might he have acted some cardboard jackbooted Prussian in an end-of-term comedy at Hyderabad House near Bridport.
The house floated with tears and terror and uncontainable fury and music that made children dream of the jackbooted intruders who lit their way with torches made of Jewish hair.
Despite the images of jackbooted Nazis that so many students in the English-speaking world still associate with the country, Germany has been utterly transformed.

senses: Manioc (Manihot esculenta), a tropical plant which is the source of tapioca.
The root of this plant.
Tapioca, a starchy pulp made with manioc roots.
ety: Borrowed from Spanish cazabe, from Taíno *kasabi (“cassava flour”) (whence Garifuna sibiba), from Proto-Arawak *sapi.
examples: There was a smell of evening and of coolness after a hot day and a slight scent of peat-smoke that came from cassava being roasted in one of the fishermen's huts in the village away to the right.

senses: Dimly lit, as at dusk (evening).
Having a shade of color that is rather dark.
Dark-skinned.
Ashen; having a greyish skin coloration.
ety: From dusk + -y.
examples: I like it when it is dusky, just before the street lights come on.
A beech wood with silver firs in it rolled down the face of the hill, and the maze of leafless twigs and dusky spires cut sharp against the soft blueness of the evening sky.
The dusky rose was of a muted color, not clashing with any of the other colors.

senses: A small bowl or container, sometimes with a cover such as a Tupperware container.
A small pick-up truck or ute, generally open and sometimes fitted with a removable canopy, but distinct from an enclosed van and a large truck.
ety: Borrowed from Afrikaans bakkie, and then either: * from Northern Dutch bakkie (informal), from Dutch bakje (“container; drinking vessel; (archaic) carriage for passengers”), from bak (“container; drinking vessel; vehicle; part of a vehicle for carrying loads; part of a carriage for carrying passengers”) (see further at that entry) + -je (diminutive suffix); or * from Afrikaans bak (“container; part of a vehicle for carrying loads”) (from Dutch bak; see above) + -ie (diminutive suffix).
examples: The "Noria" pump is a bucket-and-chain arrangement, well known, I believe, in the Cape Colony as the "bakkies" pump; it is very effective for it lifts from 10 feet to 30 feet.

senses: Having a rind or skin.
ety: From rind + -y.
examples: If you graff upon a large Stock that may pinch your Graff, let the inner and woody Part of your Graff bear the Pressure, by being a little thicker than the rindy Part

senses: A shop selling perfumes.
A factory where perfume is made.
The manufacture of perfume.
ety: From perfume + -ery.
examples: These perfumeries were also used as places of assignation and sexual rendezvous.

senses: Any of several primitive fish, of the family Polyodontidae, that have a long snout shaped like a paddle.
The American paddlefish.
ety: From paddle + fish.
examples: Caviar comes from various species of sturgeons and paddlefishes.

senses: Out of place, incompatible, inharmonious, not congruent.
ety: From in- + congruent.
examples: The yellow blazer was incongruent for the funeral.
Her knowledge of world politics was incongruent in someone so young.
And like so many robots, they’re an incongruent mashup of terrifying and cute. Aww, look at those guys. Also, runnnnn!

senses: The Chinese tropical fruit tree Litchi chinensis, of the soapberry family.
That tree's bright red oval fruit with a single stone surrounded by a fleshy white aril.
A soft pink-red colour, like that of a lychee rind (also called lychee red).
ety: * /ˈlaɪ̯.t͡ʃi/, /laɪ̯ˈt͡ʃiː/ from Cantonese 荔枝 (lai⁶ zi¹) * /ˈlit͡ʃi/ from Hokkien 荔枝 (lē-chi) Doublet of litchi and lichi.
examples: No Chinese meal is complete without some succulent dim sims (pork minced with water chestnuts and enclosed in paste), and such sweets as honeyed lychee nuts and honeyed ginger.

senses: A bar (drinking establishment) equipped with video arcade games.
ety: Blend of bar + arcade. A chain of arcade bars by this name first opened in Brooklyn in 2004.
examples: Glen “Hooping Cough” Hodges is proprietor and manager of Nine Chakras, the new retro gaming barcade in town.
Gaming itself becomes a destination event, taking place at barcades and board game cafes.

senses: Crystals of silicon carbide used as an abrasive.
ety: Blend of carbon + corundum; originally a trade name.
examples: There is no doubt that such a button — properly prepared under great pressure — of carborundum, especially of powder of the best quality, will withstand the effect of the bombardment fully as well as anything we know.
This can most readily be done by use of carborundum marking. The procedure involves successive marking of the same mat with layers of carborundum at least twice.
At the same times, samples were taken to determine that the carborundum treatment did increase the amount of wear of the mandibles compared with insects on the diet without carborundum powder.

senses: The state of being illogical or absurd.
The state of being incapable of reason or abstract thought.
Something that is irrational; the result of an illogical or absurd thought or action.
ety: From irrational + -ity. May also be analyzed as ir- + rationality.
examples: Man introduces reason into the world of Nature, destroying irrational struggle and waste. But this activity is outside of self, distant, only reflected. Man sees this irrationality only with his intellect.

senses: To move smoothly from one state or subject to another.
To make a smooth transition from one theme to another.
To play a sequence of records with no talk between them.
ety: Borrowed from Italian segue (“it follows”), from seguire (“to follow”), from Latin sequor; originally a term used in a musical score to indicate that the next movement or passage is to follow without a break. Cognate with Spanish seguir. Doublet of sue. Related to suit and sequence.
examples: I can tell she’s going to segue from our conversation about school to the topic of marriage.
Then, in a staggering display of empathy for the deceased lacking, this friend segues to the narcissist nub of the matter: "Omg wat if yu get arrested b4 yur bdai."
Beethoven’s symphonies effortlessly segue from one theme to the next.

senses: An Arctic toothed whale (Monodon monoceros) that grows to about 20 feet (6 meters) long, the male having a single horn-like tusk, a twisted, pointed cuspid that projects forward.
ety: From Dutch narwal or Danish/Norwegian Bokmål narhval, from Old Norse náhvalr, from nár (“corpse”) + hvalr (“whale”). Compare Icelandic náhvalur.
examples: Moreover, both narwhals and bowheads can occur in late summer in southern Prince Regent Inlet (coming from Lancaster Sound) and may reach Fury and Hecla Strait and northern Foxe Basin.
At over 2.5 m in length, the tusk of the male narwhal (Monodon monoceros) is one the most impressive instruments of male-male competition among mammals.

senses: To cause to be more lively, or to become more lively.
ety: Partly from life + -en; partly from live (adjective) + -en; and partly a shortening of enliven. Cognate with Norwegian Nynorsk livna (“to quicken, come alive”), Faroese livna (“to come to life, come alive”), Icelandic lifna (“to come to life”).
examples: The fact of this made him realize he had a story. He livened. Father was washed overboard, Rupert said. He was going through the water like a duck.

senses: A treatment with a salt solution.
The increase of salt content in soil.
The increase of salt content in water.
ety: From salinate + -ion.
examples: Such extension of control diminishes disturbances of the peace, stabilises and thus promotes agricultural industry, and puts a check on the exhaustion and salination of the soil.

senses: Truth, particularly of a transcendent character.
ety: Borrowed from Latin vēritās. Doublet of verity.
examples: Over at Harvard, students are pursuing a different kind of sexual veritas.

senses: Someone who uses irony in humor.
A supporter of ironism.
ety: From irony + -ist.
examples: The great ironists do not merely use irony: they live ironically.

senses: Acting suspiciously; strange, unusual; acting in a manner as if having something to hide, or seemingly crooked.
Suspicious (of something).
Dishonest; sketchy; shady
Unreliable; wonky
Snobbish; haughty
ety: Possibly from obsolete Scots hink, from Old Norse hinka (“to limp or hobble”), probably not from Old English inca (“doubt; suspicion”). Possibly from hank (“a loop or coil or anything that curbs or restrains”). Possibly from African-American usage: hincty or hinkty.
examples: I thought he might be acting hinky.
There's nothing hinky about this.
And I don't know if that copper reaction you teased me with for H2CO3 would run that direction, would it? Looks hinky.

senses: Like paste, sticky.
Pale, lacking colour, having a pallor.
ety: From paste + -y (adjectival suffix).
examples: These mashed potatoes aren’t cooked well; they are very pasty.
Are you feeling OK? You look a bit pasty.

senses: To rebuke harshly.
ety: From Dutch kielhalen (“keelhaul”), from kiel (“keel”) + halen (“fetch; catch”).
examples: Time keelhauls me and what happens meanwhile is: nothing. No more voice, no more orders.

senses: A formal demand made by one state or government upon another for the surrender or extradition of a fugitive from justice.
A formal application by one officer to another for things needed in the public service.
That which is required by authority; especially, a quota of supplies or necessaries.
A call; an invitation; a summons.
ety: From Middle English requisicion, from Old French requisicion, from Medieval Latin requisitio. By surface analysis, requisit(e) + -ion.
examples: Amid the many mirrors called into requisition by Lady Townshend's fête, not one gave back a lovelier likeness than that which reflected the face and form of Lady Marchmont.

senses: Close to the number forty
About forty years old.
ety: From forty + -ish.
examples: I’m going to start a support group of us fortyish guys with this problem. LUMPS, we’ll call our group. Losing Unwanted Midriff Plumpitude Sensibly.

senses: A form of lava flow of basaltic rock, usually dark-colored with a smooth or ropey surface. It is one of two chief forms of lava flow emitted from volcanoes of the Hawaiian type, the other form being aa.
ety: Borrowed from Hawaiian pāhoehoe.
examples: The twisty, ropy kind that personifies flow – all congealed motion – is called pahoehoe.

senses: An act of venturing out to do a task, etc.
An act of trying to enter a new field of activity.
A series of aerial photographs taken during the flight of an aircraft; (by extension) a photography session.
ety: The verb is derived from the noun.
examples: Finally, the astronauts will descend to the lunar surface. After their sortie on the moon, they'll return to the orbital station.

senses: The characteristic of being a man; maleness; masculinity; manliness; manhood.
ety: From Middle English manship (“position of honor; respect; courtesy; manly spirit or conduct; humanity; human condition”), from Old English mansċipe (“humanity, courtesy”), equivalent to man + -ship. Cognate with Dutch manschap (“homage, manred, crew”), German Mannschaft (“team, crew, squad, force”), Swedish manskap (“rank, crew”).
examples: He certainly had nothing to do with the choosing of his manship, any more than his sister had of her womanhood.
The manship of Jesus was hid from the eyes of men as completely as the Godship.

senses: A cry of encouragement; an accolade.
ety: A variant pronunciation of That's the boy!, a cry of encouragement, especially to children and pet dogs.
examples: LOS ANGELES, June 29 — Drink in hand, attaboys coming at him from every direction, Tom DeSanto was living the fanboy dream.

senses: Crazy, insane.
Fraught or out of control.
Obsessed; overly enthusiastic.
Ridiculous; unbelievable or silly.
ety: From nuts + -o.
examples: How being taught to not cut corners, even in a nutso emergency room shift, meant I checked all regions in Mary below the waist and didn't just tell her I thought it was probably gas.
I put my hand to my chest—my heart was going nutso.
A nutso relationship is no joke, and no baby should be exposed to that.

senses: To shine, gleam.
ety: Perhaps onomatopoeic; perhaps an error for, or a nonce alteration of, blink or click; perhaps a continuation of Middle English bliken (compare blicker), which may have survived in dialect despite not being attested in print for 500 years.
examples: Shirley Steynes Bluey took a deep breath as he entered the main street; nothing new under the sun-lamp as white pinks blicked across the street in a line of heat-glazed asterisks
The lancing sunlight blicked sharps of light from the scattering of sand on the marble of the plinth.

senses: A small spiked wheel on the end of a spur of certain types.
A little flat ring or wheel on a horse's bit.
A roll of hair, silk, etc., passed through the flesh of a horse in the manner of a seton in human surgery.
ety: From Middle English rowel, rowell, rowelle, from Old French roel, roiele (compare modern French rouelle), from Late Latin rotella, diminutive of Latin rota (“wheel”). Doublet of rotella.
examples: The dry desert of my native land, her men grey and gaunt, their spines twisted, their feet shod with rowel and spur.
The Lone Ranger will storm in at the head of a posse, rowels tearing blood from the stallion’s white hide, to find his young friend, innocent Dan, swinging from a tree limb by a broken neck.
He nodded at the Americans. Buena suerte, he said. He put the long rowels of his spurs to the horse and they moved on.

senses: A blow that produces a muffled sound.
The sound of such a blow; a thud.
Synonym of bump (“sudden movement of underground strata”).
ety: Mid 16th century, probably imitative.
examples: The watchman gave so very great a thump at my door last night, that I awakened at the knock.

senses: Any of several irises that have a fragrant root, especially Iris × germanica.
The fragrant root of such an iris.
ety: Probably from iris, although the alteration of the vowel is unexplained.
examples: Drop twelve drops of genuine oil of rhodium on a lump of loaf-sugar ; grind this wel in a glass mortar, and mix it thoroughly with three pounds of orris powder.
Next place your hair, the rose quartz, some of the orris root powder, and the candle drippings into the box.
